title: Sub-2-bit quantization fits a second 20B-class model under 5 GB by Q2 2027
body: PrismML released Bonsai 27B on July 14 in two extreme-quantization builds: a ternary variant at 1.71 effective bits per weight and 5.9 GB that retains 95% of its full-precision baseline across 15 benchmarks, and a 1-bit binary variant at 1.125 effective bits per weight and 3.9 GB that retains 90%. The second is the point of the exercise, because 3.9 GB fits inside the roughly 6 GB of usable memory an iPhone 17 Pro leaves for model weights — a budget that had kept 27B-class weights off handsets entirely. On-device inference has been bounded by memory rather than compute, and the standard workaround was to shrink the model until the capability went with it, which is why the portable tier has been populated by small models instead of flagship-class ones. Bonsai inverts that trade: it keeps a 27B-class model derived from Qwen3.6 27B and pays for the memory fit with a 5-10% benchmark tax rather than a parameter cut. Two things should make the result travel rather than stay a one-off. The weights are Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face and GitHub, so the artifact is inspectable by anyone trying to reproduce the encoding. And the incentive is general: every open-weight family — Gemma, Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek — has the same memory wall between it and a handset, and whoever clears it first sets which of their models counts as portable. The counterweight is cost: post-training quantization degrades sharply below roughly 3 bits, so holding 90% at 1.125 bits generally implies quantization-aware training or distillation at real expense, which narrows the field to funded labs and big-tech research groups rather than the hobbyist quantization community — slower, but far from empty. The prediction: by Q2 2027, at least one group other than PrismML publishes open weights for a model of at least 20B parameters encoded at 2.0 or fewer effective bits per weight, occupying no more than 5 GB on disk, with a published multi-benchmark evaluation reporting at least 90% retention against its own full-precision baseline. What this does not claim is a phone demonstration: Bonsai's 134 and 163 tokens per second were measured on an RTX 5090 rather than a handset, so the iPhone case is a memory-fit argument, not a throughput result — the forecast turns on the encoding replicating, not on a device shipping one.

reasoning.because: PrismML's Bonsai 27B hits 1.125 bits/weight, 3.9 GB, ~90% retention, Apache-2.0 open weights
reasoning.given: On-device inference is memory-bound, so bits per weight sets which model class counts as portable
reasoning.so_that: A second group publishes an open-weight ≥20B model at ≤2 effective bits/weight, ≤5 GB, ≥90% benchmark retention
reasoning.landing: by Q2 2027; a second group ships a ≥20B model at ≤2 bits/weight, ≤5 GB
reasoning.plain_language: A startup shrank a big AI model enough to fit in a phone's memory without losing much skill. Another team will copy that soon.

summary: PrismML's Bonsai 27B holds 90% of its full-precision baseline at 1.125 bits per weight and 3.9 GB — inside a phone's memory budget. Because on-device inference is bounded by memory, not compute, expect a second group to publish a 20B+ open-weight model under 2 bits per weight and 5 GB by Q2 2027.
